objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain normal, cold, hot, flooded, night and external power starts, the starter and oil limits that apply during a start, and propeller safety, and you can teach a learner to position the airplane, run the start checklist and spot and fix the errors learners make.
why: Engine starting is the first time in every lesson that your learner controls a running propeller, and the propeller is nearly invisible once it turns [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. The habits you set here last: a major objective of primary training is to build habit patterns that serve pilots for a whole career [[24:36|AFH 1-15]], and learners copy their instructor's safety practices whether they mean to or not [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

prereading.what: Clearing the area, brakes and throttle on start, oil pressure and starter limits, the stuck starter, and hand propping step by step.
prereading.label: AFH 2-16 to 2-17

prereading.what: Ignition system and the switch-off hazard, oil pressure and temperature on start, the starting circuit and start safety.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-15 to 7-19

prereading.what: Fuel injection hot starts, the primer and overpriming, vapor lock, and starting with a ground power unit.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-12 to 7-30

prereading.what: Turbine starts in brief: battery voltage, an adequate GPU, hot starts and hung starts.
prereading.label: AFH 15-10, 15-12

prereading.what: Demonstration-performance and telling-and-doing, the way to teach a procedure like a start.
prereading.label: AIH 9-5 to 9-8

prereading.what: A runaway engine on start, and instructional risk management with the learner on the controls.
prereading.label: AIH 1-1, 10-6 to 10-8

prereading.what: Likelihood, severity and the risk assessment matrix, for weighing start hazards.
prereading.label: RMH 4-1 to 4-2

warmup: Think first: on a 25 degree F morning your learner is about to make her first start in a fuel-injected airplane. A line worker rolls up a ground power cart and stands beside the nose waiting to plug it in. What do you brief before anyone touches the starter, who stands where, and which gauge do you both watch first once the engine fires?

key_terms.def: A heavy switch the ignition key energizes in START. Until it closes, the starter motor gets no power even with the battery on.
A clutch in the starter drive that lets the engine run faster than the starter, so the running engine does not drive the starter motor.
An engine-driven unit with a permanent magnet that makes its own spark current, with no need for the airplane's battery or master switch.
The wire that grounds the magneto to turn the ignition off. If it is broken, the engine can fire with the switch OFF.
A plug on the airplane through which a ground power unit can supply electrical power for starting.
A ground unit (the AFH glossary calls it a type of small gas turbine) that supplies electrical power, air pressure or both for starting engines.
A pump that sprays fuel directly into the cylinders before a start. Helpful in the cold; too much is overpriming.
Fuel vapor or air in the fuel system that keeps fuel from reaching the cylinders and makes a restart hard or impossible.
Starting an engine by pulling the propeller through by hand. A two-person procedure from the AFM/POH.
A turbine start in which exhaust temperature exceeds its limit. Not the same as starting a hot piston engine.
A turbine start that accelerates too slowly and settles at an rpm too low for the engine to keep running without the starter.
Instructor tells and does, learner tells and instructor does, learner tells and does, then learner does and the instructor evaluates.

body.p: Engine starting looks like a few switches, but it is the first hazard of every flight. Engines vary a lot, so the actual procedure always comes from the approved start checklist in the AFM/POH; the AFH adds some generally accepted hazard mitigation practices [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Your job is to teach the learner to read the POH procedure, understand why each step is there, and run it the same way every time.

head: What the ACS asks
What it means for you
rows: K1 to K3: describe and explain starting under various conditions, with external power, and the engine limits that relate to starting (ACS AI.V.C)
You explain the system and the limits in plain words, not just recite the checklist.
R1 to R3: explain and teach how to manage propeller, external power and starting limit risks (ACS AI.V.C)
You teach the risk, not only avoid it yourself.
S1, S2: demonstrate and simultaneously explain positioning the airplane and completing the checklist (ACS AI.V.C)
You narrate the start from your seat as you would to a learner.

body.p: At a minimum, prepared checklists cover the before engine start and engine starting phases [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. Checklist use is evaluated throughout the practical test (ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: Learners imitate their instructor, and your description of safety practices means little if you do not show them every time [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. Shout CLEAR, wait for an answer and hold the brakes on every start you make, even on a deserted ramp.

check.q: Where does the procedure for starting a particular airplane come from, and what do the handbooks add?
check.a: The approved engine start checklist in the AFM/POH; the handbooks add generally accepted hazard mitigation practices [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

chunks.title: The starting system, explained for a learner

body.p: Most small airplanes use a direct-cranking electric starter: a source of electricity, wiring, switches, solenoids and the starter motor [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. Teach it as a chain the learner can trace on the diagram.

bullets: Battery switch ON: power reaches the main bus through the battery solenoid [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
The starter does nothing yet. It runs only when the key in START energizes the starting solenoid [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Release the key: the solenoid removes power from the starter motor [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Once the engine runs, a clutch in the starter drive lets the engine turn faster than the starter, so the engine does not drive the starter motor [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].
Power can come from the onboard battery or from external power through an external power receptacle [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

body.p: The ignition is a separate system. A magneto makes its own current, completely independent of the airplane's electrical system, and fires whenever the crankshaft turns [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]. The key has five positions: OFF, R, L, BOTH and START [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

This is the most important idea in the lesson for propeller safety. With the ignition switch left ON, the engine can fire when the propeller is moved, even with the battery and master switches OFF. And if the ground wire between a magneto and the switch is broken, the engine can fire with the switch OFF [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

callout.text: Battery turns the starter. Magnetos make the spark. The master switch does not control the magnetos [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

Application: have the learner trace the circuit on the diagram with a finger, from the battery to the starter, before the first start. Then ask what turns the spark on and off. Do not move on until the answer is "the magneto switch, not the master."

check.q: Your learner says, "The master is off, so the propeller is safe to move." What do you teach?
check.a: The master switch does not power the ignition. Magnetos need no outside power, so the engine can fire if the propeller is moved with the ignition ON, or with it OFF if a ground wire is broken [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]] [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].

body.p: The ACS does not list the conditions, so teach the ones the sources describe and send the learner to the POH for each exact procedure. Every row below starts with the POH.

head: Condition
What the sources say
What to teach
rows: Brakes held, a hand on the throttle, about 1,000 rpm after start, and oil pressure up within about 30 seconds [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
The baseline. Teach it first and teach the others as changes to it.

Use the proper seasonal oil grade and preheat as temperatures approach and fall below freezing [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. In the cold there is not enough heat to vaporize fuel in the carburetor, so the primer helps [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]. Fuel injection gives easier cold weather starts [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].
Build preheat time into the schedule. Expect oil temperature to stay low for several minutes after start [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

Fuel injection's listed disadvantages include difficulty starting a hot engine and vapor locks during ground operations on hot days [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. On fuel-injected engines the fuel can get so hot it vaporizes in the line [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]].
No handbook gives a piston hot engine procedure. Use the POH one. Warn the learner that the term "hot start" means something else on a turbine.

Overpriming is a hazard of the primer; read the airplane's priming instructions to avoid it [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]. Excessive throttle after the engine fires is the main cause of backfiring during a start [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
The handbooks give no flooded start procedure. Teach the POH one, and teach smooth throttle once the engine fires.
Anticollision lights on before every start, and position lights too at night [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Position lights must be lit when operating from sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]].
Application: a flashlight walk-around of the propeller area before start.
Running a tank dry can let air into the fuel system and cause vapor lock that makes a restart difficult [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]].
Teach tank management so the learner never meets this one.
A GPU is very useful, especially for cold weather starting; follow the manufacturer's procedure [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].
Taught in its own chunk below.

For airplanes built without an electric starter, per the AFM/POH, by competent people [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; a team of two trained people [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. A broken starter calls for a mechanic [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Taught in its own chunk below.

body.p: Turbine engines, in brief: temperatures are hotter during starting than at any other time, and a start whose temperature exceeds the limit is a hot start; one that accelerates too slowly and hangs below self-sustaining speed is a hung or false start, often from low battery power [[24:306|AFH 15-12]].

callout.text: Do not let a learner merge two different ideas. The PHAK speaks of difficulty starting a hot fuel-injected piston engine [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. The AFH and PHAK use the term "hot start" only for turbines: a start in which exhaust temperature exceeds its limit, which can do serious engine damage [[24:306|AFH 15-12]] [[24:380|AFH G-8]] [[1:183|PHAK 7-23]].

check.q: Why is a fuel-injected engine often easier to start cold but harder to start hot?
check.a: The PHAK lists easier cold weather starts as an advantage of fuel injection, and difficulty starting a hot engine and vapor lock on hot days as disadvantages [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]; the fuel can vaporize in the lines [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]].

chunks.title: Teaching each start with the POH

body.p: A start is a procedure, so teach it with the demonstration-performance method: explanation, demonstration, learner performance with instructor supervision, and evaluation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. In the airplane it becomes telling-and-doing.

head: Step
Applied to engine starting
rows: Open the POH together. Read the normal, cold, hot and flooded procedures and say why each step is there. Cover safety and invite questions [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
You make the first start, narrating each step in the same order you explained it. Demonstrate it exactly the way the learner should do it, safety steps included [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
The learner calls each step while you do it. Misunderstandings show up before the learner is busy with the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
The learner starts while thinking out loud; you watch for errors and stay ready to take control [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Learner self-assessment first, then yours, compared in discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

body.p: Build from simple to complex: the normal start first, then the variations, so the learner gains confidence before the harder cases [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A learner may not meet a hot or flooded engine during training. Use visualization: have the learner talk through a normal start, then add a problem such as a hot, fuel-injected engine that will not catch, and ask questions about how they would handle it [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

callout.text: Before you teach in a model you do not know, review its POH or get time in it first [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Engines vary substantially [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], so read the start section before every new type.

check.q: Your learner has never seen a hot, fuel-injected start. How do you teach it before it happens on a real summer day?
check.a: Read the POH hot start procedure on the ground, then use visualization: the learner talks through a normal start and you add the hot engine that will not catch, asking questions about each step [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

body.p: Some airplanes have a receptacle for an external ground power unit (GPU). It provides electrical energy for starting and is very useful, especially in cold weather [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. The AFH glossary defines a GPU as a type of small gas turbine that supplies electrical power, air pressure or both for starting [[24:380|AFH G-8]].

On the circuit diagram the external power plug feeds the main bus through an external power relay [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]]. Have the learner find both parts on f1 and say where the starter gets its power during a GPU start.

head: Teach
Source
rows: The exact GPU start sequence comes only from the POH
Follow the manufacturer's recommendations for a GPU start [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].
A cold engine is hard to start [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]], and a GPU is very useful in cold weather starting [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]].
Turbine starts depend on the right minimum battery voltage or a GPU of adequate output [[24:306|AFH 15-12]]; low voltage makes a hot start more likely [[24:304|AFH 15-10]].
Low voltage, high ammeter or loadmeter readings, dim lights or radio noise after start can mean the starter is still running [[18:1|AC 91-55A]].

callout.text: Application: a GPU is often used because the battery is weak. Ask the learner what that battery will do for the rest of the flight. The sources do not answer it, so the answer is the POH and a mechanic, not a guess.

check.q: Where on the PHAK starting circuit does external power join the system?
check.a: The external power plug feeds the main bus through an external power relay [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]]; the starter then draws from the main bus [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

body.p: The sources say little about GPU risks beyond following the manufacturer [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. So teach it the way the AIH teaches all risk: identify the hazard, assess it, and decide how to mitigate it [[25:7|AIH 1-3]]. The hazards below are application, built on what the sources do say.

head: Hazard
Why it matters
Mitigation to teach
rows: A person working at the nose
Whoever plugs in or pulls the cord works close to a propeller that is nearly invisible once it turns [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Agree how the cord will be pulled and from which side, approach from behind the propeller arc as with chocks [[24:54|AFH 2-17]], and use agreed signals [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].
Cart or cord in the propeller arc or blast
Prop blast can throw objects and hurt people or property [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Cart parked clear of the arc and the blast; check before start.
Only the manufacturer's procedure is approved [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]
Read the POH GPU procedure aloud and follow it as a checklist.
Low power increases the chance of a hot or hung start [[24:304|AFH 15-10]] [[24:306|AFH 15-12]]
Confirm the GPU output meets the AFM before start.
Know the normal readings; shut down if they change [[18:1|AC 91-55A]].

body.p: Line workers and signals: the AFH shows standard hand signals including start engines, pull chocks and cut engines. Which set is used matters less than an agreed-upon set [[24:52|AFH 2-15]]. Before the start, agree with the person at the GPU what signal means "disconnected and clear."

callout.text: Application: never let the learner taxi until the ground worker, the cart and the cord are clear and the disconnect is confirmed by an agreed signal.

check.q: A line worker plugs in a GPU at the nose and then needs to unplug it with the engine running. What do you brief?
check.a: Agreed signals [[24:52|AFH 2-15]], approach only from behind the propeller arc because the propeller is nearly invisible [[24:54|AFH 2-17]], and the POH sequence for disconnecting [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. Note that the sources give no GPU-specific approach rule; this is applied from the chocks rule.

chunks.title: Engine limits that apply during a start

head: Limit
Source value
Why
rows: Avoid cranking longer than 30 seconds without a cool-down of at least 30 seconds to 1 minute; some POHs specify longer [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Starters are not built for continuous duty; heat damages them. A burning insulation smell suggests the limit was exceeded [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Seek advice from a qualified person [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Keep cranking and you trade a fixable problem for a burned starter.
The POH setting; in general about 1,000 rpm [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Lets oil pressure rise and limits wear from poor lubrication at high rpm [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
In most conditions at least the lower limit within 30 seconds; if not, shut down immediately [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Serious internal damage is likely if the limits are not reached and held [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Oil temperature rises slowly after a cold start [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].
Propeller in full low pitch, nose into the wind, cowl flaps open [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Air cooling is less effective on the ground [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].
A continuous very high ammeter reading, or a starter engaged light, means the starter stayed engaged: shut down [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
A stuck relay can overload and overheat the system and destroy the starter drive [[18:1|AC 91-55A]].

body.p: Read the gauges with the learner before the first start. A plus ammeter reading is the battery's charging rate; a full-scale minus deflection means an alternator or generator malfunction, and a full-scale plus deflection means a regulator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. Right after start a high charge that falls as the battery recovers is expected (application); one that stays very high is the stuck-starter sign.

callout.text: Limits in this table are the handbook's general values. The POH values for your airplane win, and some POHs set longer starter cool-downs [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

check.q: Your learner cranks for 25 seconds, pauses 10 seconds, and cranks again for 25 seconds. What limit did she break, and what is the fix?
check.a: The cool-down. After a long crank the AFH calls for at least 30 seconds to 1 minute of cooling [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; the POH may require longer.

chunks.title: Managing starting limits while you teach

body.p: The AIH opens with a real start that went wrong. On engine start the rpm ran past 2,000; the learner said she had pulled the throttle back, and the instructor and learner both grabbed the mixture and pulled it to stop the engine. The throttle rod end had been left unsecured after an annual inspection [[25:5|AIH 1-1]].

Lessons for the instructor: keep a hand near the throttle and know the mixture is the backup stop, just as idle cutoff is the only way to stop an engine that runs with a broken magneto ground wire [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. With a learner on the controls, the learner manipulating the controls may itself be a significant hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]], and on first attempts you stay alert and ready to take control [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

head: Sign during or after start
What to do
Source
rows: Oil pressure not up in about 30 seconds
Very high continuous ammeter, starter light
Low voltage, dim lights, radio noise
Shut down; no flight until fixed
Unusual sounds, vibrations, smells or smoke
Stop cranking; the starter limit was exceeded

body.p: Use the risk matrix to show the learner why these are no-go items. Risk is the composite of likelihood and severity, and a high or serious result means no-go unless the risk can be reduced [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

callout.text: Agree in the briefing who calls the shutdown and how. Application: "If either of us says SHUT DOWN, mixture to idle cutoff, no discussion." In the AIH story both people reached for the mixture at once [[25:5|AIH 1-1]]; a briefed plan removes doubt about who does it.

check.q: In the AIH story, what stopped the runaway engine, and why does it matter for your briefing?
check.a: Pulling the mixture [[25:5|AIH 1-1]]. The mixture to idle cutoff is the backup stop when the throttle or the ignition cannot stop the engine [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]], so brief who pulls it and when.

chunks.title: Propeller safety around learners and passengers

body.p: Teach the propeller as a constant hazard, with and without the engine running.

head: When
What to teach
Source
rows: Area clear of persons, equipment and hazards; check behind the airplane; anticollision lights on; call CLEAR out the window and wait for a response
No one near the propeller; wheels chocked and brakes set
Brakes held so the airplane cannot lunge forward; hand on the throttle
The propeller is nearly invisible. Chocks are approached only from behind the propeller, with the throttle at idle, never from the front or side
Keep people, ground equipment and other aircraft out of the propeller wash during warm-up
Check the magneto grounding in OFF at idle; switch the ignition OFF when the engine stops
Always assume the ignition is on

body.p: Passengers and learners. Passengers may have little ramp experience, so they move only as directed or with an escort [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Serious injuries and deaths have happened when people who had just started an engine walked or reached into the propeller arc to pull chocks, reach the cabin or go toward the tail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Teach the learner to brief passengers to stay clear and to board and leave only with the engine stopped (application).

callout.text: No person may operate an aircraft in a careless or reckless manner so as to endanger the life or property of another [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(a)]]. Paragraph (b) applies the same rule on the surface of an airport used by aircraft for air commerce, even when the operation is not for air navigation [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(b)]].

No person may operate an aircraft equipped with an anticollision light system unless the anticollision lights are lighted. They need not be lighted when the PIC determines that, because of operating conditions, turning them off is in the interest of safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(b)]]. Teaching them on before every start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] also warns the ramp that the propeller is about to move (application).

check.q: A passenger wants to hop out to grab a forgotten bag while the engine idles. What do you teach the learner to say?
check.a: No. Shut down first. The propeller is nearly invisible and people have been killed walking into the arc to reach the cabin or chocks [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]; passengers move on the ramp only as directed [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

chunks.title: Hand propping: teach it as a team procedure

body.p: Most airplanes have electric starters, and an airworthy airplane's starter should work; if it does not, call a certificated mechanic. Hand propping is for vintage airplanes built without a starter, done per the AFM/POH and only by competent people. The consequences of getting it wrong are serious to fatal [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

head: Element
Standard
Source
rows: Two trained people who know the airplane; the person out front directs. Someone unfamiliar with the controls never sits in the pilot's seat
Stable, free of gravel, wet grass, grease, mud, oil, ice or snow; otherwise move the airplane
Fuel and engine controls set for a normal start; magneto switch checked OFF
Descending blade slightly above horizontal; face it squarely, slightly less than an arm's length away
FUEL ON, SWITCH OFF, THROTTLE CLOSED, BRAKES SET; then BRAKES AND CONTACT, each repeated back after checking
Push the blade down rapidly with the palms, not gripped fingers, and step back
Do not reposition the blade until the magneto switch is verified OFF

body.p: The words CONTACT and SWITCH OFF are used because they sound very different in noise or wind [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Gripping the blade can draw the body into the propeller if the engine misfires, kicks back or turns backward [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Standing too far away makes the person lean forward off balance and risks a fall into the blades [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

callout.text: Teach that hand propping is hazardous even when done perfectly [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. As an instructor, you decide whether it happens at all. A broken starter on a starter-equipped trainer is a maintenance squawk, not a hand propping lesson [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

check.q: Your tailwheel learner, in a vintage airplane with no starter, offers to let his non-pilot friend sit in the left seat during hand propping. What do you say?
check.a: No. The seat occupant must be trained and familiar with the airplane and controls; a person unfamiliar with the controls should never occupy the pilot's seat [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

body.p: The ACS asks you to position the airplane considering structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property (ACS AI.V.C.S1). Teach each one by name.

head: Consider
What to look for
Source
rows: What is behind the airplane: hangars, open doors, parked cars. Propeller thrust can accelerate objects to high speed
Do not point your blast at them. Prop wash and jet blast cause damage and upsets at close range, and large aircraft can overturn small ones
Ground running is done with the nose into the wind for best cooling. When you park, head into the existing or forecast wind when you can
Clear of persons and equipment that could contact the airplane or propeller; CLEAR called and answered
Avoid spots where the propeller will stir up gravel or dust, to protect the propeller and property

body.p: Positioning starts when the learner parks after the last flight. Teach them to park in a spot and heading where other airplanes' blast will not strike it, headed into the wind, then roll straight ahead to straighten the nosewheel [[24:60|AFH 2-23]]. If the tiedown position leaves the tail toward a hangar or the propeller over gravel, push the airplane before the start rather than starting where it sits (application).
Rotating beacons on large aircraft warn that their engines run, but it is a voluntary program; do not rely only on the beacon [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

callout.text: On the ramp, have the learner walk a full circle and name each of the five considerations out loud, pointing at the hazard. It turns S1 into a habit you can see.

check.q: Your learner positions the airplane and says only, "Nobody is near the propeller." Which ACS S1 considerations did she leave out?
check.a: Structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby property. S1 lists structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property (ACS AI.V.C.S1).

body.p: A checklist is a memory aid. You may do the actions and then use the checklist to confirm them, with the emphasis on the check; but checklists have no value if the pilot is not committed to them [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

head: Checklist
Items the sources add (always the POH first)
rows: Radio equipment switches OFF [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]; anticollision lights ON, position lights at night [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; brakes set, area clear, behind checked [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
CLEAR called and answered; brakes held; hand on the throttle; starter within its time limit [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

Throttle to the POH rpm, about 1,000; oil pressure within 30 seconds; ammeter shows the starter disengaged [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Then gyros and suction, engine instruments, radios set [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: For a learner, the after-start scan has an order of urgency: oil pressure first, because it has a time limit [[24:54|AFH 2-17]], then the ammeter for a stuck starter [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], then the rest. If reading the checklist during the start would be unsafe, review it once conditions permit (ACS Appendix 2).

callout.text: Primer: lock it when not in use. A loose primer can vibrate open in flight and make the mixture too rich [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]]. Make "primer locked" a spoken after-start item.

check.q: Where does the IFH put the radios in the start sequence?
check.a: Radio equipment switches OFF before engine start [[23:131|IFH 5-36]], then checked for proper operation and set after start [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. The IFH does not give the reason, so do not invent one; check the POH.

chunks.title: How to teach it: an engine start lesson

head: Phase
What you do
rows: Objective and completion standard, the POH start procedures, propeller safety, and the exchange of controls [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[24:37|AFH 1-16]]. Brief who calls a shutdown.
Learner positions or checks the airplane against the five S1 items and briefs passengers [[24:51|AFH 2-14]] (ACS AI.V.C.S1).
You tell and do: narrate every step, CLEAR, brakes, throttle, oil pressure [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
Learner tells while you do, then learner tells and does, thinking out loud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Cold, hot, flooded and GPU starts by POH reading and visualization, then real ones as the season allows [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].
Learner self-assessment, then yours, compared in discussion [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

body.p: Teach before you start the engine, not during it. Avoid teaching at an inappropriate time, and discuss hazards and risk mitigation in detail during preflight and postflight [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Once the propeller turns, your words are short: "Oil pressure?" "Ammeter?"

Watch the learner's eyes and hands during the start. Errors caused by a misconception and errors caused by a lack of motor skill look different, and thinking out loud tells you which you have [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: On your CFI checkride the S elements have no numeric tolerance. The evaluator watches whether you demonstrate and explain at the same time (ACS AI.V.C), so practice narrating the whole start out loud.

check.q: When should most of the discussion about start hazards happen, and why?
check.a: Before the start, in the preflight briefing, and again in the postflight; teaching at an inappropriate time can create a hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Tail toward an open hangar or another airplane
Check behind as standard practice; reposition [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Starter engaged without CLEAR or without waiting
Call CLEAR out the window and wait for a response [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Airplane creeps or lunges on start
High rpm right after the engine fires
Hand on the throttle; about 1,000 rpm [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; smooth throttle to avoid backfire [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]
Oil pressure in 30 seconds or shut down [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Long cranks with no pause, burning smell
30 seconds maximum, then 30 seconds to 1 minute cool-down [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]
Too many primer strokes, hard start
High ammeter, dim lights, radio whine
Ignition OFF when the engine stops [[24:60|AFH 2-23]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Someone heads for chocks or the cabin with the engine running
Idle, approach only from behind the propeller [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]

callout.text: When a learner errs, ask why it happened and what would prevent it, but do not let them practice the wrong thing [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

check.q: Your learner fires the engine and it roars to 1,800 rpm before she catches it. What do you teach?
check.a: Keep a hand on the throttle during the start and set about 1,000 rpm, or the POH value, right after start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; open the throttle slowly and smoothly while the engine is cold [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

scenario.title: A cold morning, a weak battery and a busy ramp
scenario.setup: It is 22 degrees F at 0700. Your learner, ten hours into training, is to start the school's fuel-injected trainer, which sat outside overnight. It is tied down with its tail toward an open maintenance hangar, and a larger twin is running up 100 feet to your left. The battery sounds weak on the first crank. The line worker offers a GPU and says he will stand at the nose to plug it in. Your learner's father, who came to watch, asks if he can stand by the wingtip to take a video.

questions.q: Before the learner even gets in, what should have been done about the engine in this temperature?
questions.a: Preheat is called for as temperatures approach and fall below freezing, with the proper seasonal oil grade [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Application: if it was not done, preheat now rather than crank a cold-soaked engine on a weak battery.

questions.q: How do you deal with the airplane's position?
questions.a: Check behind the airplane and avoid blowing debris into persons or property [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; the twin's prop wash can upset a light airplane at close range [[33:262|AIM 4-3-18]]. Push the airplane to a clear spot, nose into the wind if you can [[24:54|AFH 2-17]], and name the S1 items as you do it (ACS AI.V.C.S1).

questions.q: Is the GPU a good idea, and whose procedure do you use?
questions.a: A GPU is very useful for cold weather starting, and you follow the manufacturer's procedure for it [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. Read the POH GPU procedure aloud with the learner as the checklist.

questions.q: What do you brief the line worker?
questions.a: Agreed hand signals [[24:52|AFH 2-15]], and that after the start he approaches only from behind the propeller arc, which is nearly invisible when turning [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. Taxi only after the signal that the cord and cart are clear. The sources give no GPU-specific rule; this is applied from the chocks rule.

questions.q: The father wants to film from the wingtip. What do you and the learner tell him?
questions.a: The AFH has passengers move on the ramp only as directed or with an escort [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]; apply the same to a visitor (application). Keep him well clear of the propeller arc and out of the propeller wash during the start and warm-up [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

questions.q: The engine starts. The ammeter stays pegged high and the radios whine. What does your learner do, and what do you teach afterward?
questions.a: Shut down: a continuous very high ammeter reading means the starter may still be engaged [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], and radio noise and high readings after start point to a starter that keeps running; no flight until it is repaired [[18:1|AC 91-55A]]. Debrief with her self-assessment first [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

skills.do: Position the airplane properly considering structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property (ACS AI.V.C.S1). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance. The evaluator sees you check what is behind the airplane, point the blast away from hangars, people and other aircraft, consider the wind, and explain each choice out loud as you would to a learner.
skills.practice: Before every start, walk a circle and name the five S1 items out loud [[24:53|AFH 2-16]] [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. Practice explaining why you would push an airplane to a new spot rather than start where it sits.

skills.do: Complete the appropriate checklist(s) (ACS AI.V.C.S2). The ACS gives no numeric tolerance. The evaluator sees you run the before start, start and after start checklists from the POH while you demonstrate and simultaneously explain: CLEAR and wait, brakes held, hand on the throttle, about 1,000 rpm, oil pressure within 30 seconds, and the ammeter check for a disengaged starter.
skills.practice: Fly the start from the right seat with a friend in the left seat, narrating with the telling-and-doing steps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Read the cold, hot, flooded and GPU procedures in your training airplane's POH until you can explain each step [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks why the school wants tanks switched before one runs dry. Besides stopping the engine, what does the PHAK say running a tank completely dry can do?
options: Damage the electric fuel pump, which must then be replaced before the next flight
Draw sediment from the empty tank into the other one and contaminate it as well
Burn out the starter on the next start, since the engine will need longer cranking
Let air into the fuel system and cause vapor lock, which makes a restart difficult
quiz.why: Running a fuel tank completely dry may allow air to enter the fuel system and cause vapor lock, which makes it difficult to restart the engine [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]].

quiz.q: With the battery switch ON, the starter does not turn until the key reaches START. What does the PHAK say is happening?
options: The magnetos must build up a spark before the starter is allowed to turn
The master switch powers the starter only once the fuel pump is running
The starter runs only when the key in START energizes the starting solenoid
The starter waits for the battery solenoid to close after a short time delay
quiz.why: With the battery switch on, power reaches the main bus through the battery solenoid, but the starter will not operate until the starting solenoid is energized by turning the starter switch to START [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks what the fuel primer actually does. What does the PHAK say?
options: It draws fuel from the tanks and vaporizes it right into the cylinders
It pressurizes the carburetor float bowl so fuel flows faster at start
It heats the fuel in the line so it vaporizes better in cold weather
It sprays oil into the cylinders so the starter can crank more easily
quiz.why: The primer draws fuel from the tanks to vaporize fuel directly into the cylinders prior to starting; it helps in cold weather when there is not enough heat to vaporize fuel in the carburetor [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

quiz.q: On a turbine engine, what is a hung start?
options: Acceleration too slow, stabilizing below the rpm needed to run without the starter
A start in which exhaust temperature rises above its limit
A starter that stays engaged after the engine reaches self-sustaining speed
A start with too much initial fuel flow, which floods the combustor
quiz.why: A hung or false start is slower than normal acceleration that may stabilize below self-sustaining rpm, usually from low battery power or a slow starter [[24:306|AFH 15-12]].

quiz.q: A business jet sits near your start spot with its rotating beacon off. What does the AIM say about beacons and running engines?
options: A dark beacon means the engines are off, since beacons are required whenever they run
Only air carriers must use beacons, so a business jet's dark beacon means its engines are off
It is a voluntary program, so a dark beacon does not prove the engines are off
Beacons are required only at night, so a dark beacon by day means the engines are off
quiz.why: The FAA recommends that air carriers and commercial operators turn on rotating beacons whenever engines run and encourages GA pilots to do the same, but since this is a voluntary program, do not rely solely on the rotating beacon as an indication that engines are in operation [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

quiz.q: Your learner sets up for the start from memory, then reads the checklist to confirm. Per the AFH, is that acceptable?
options: No, in training every checklist must be read first and done one item at a time, never from memory
Yes, if she then uses the checklist to confirm every item, with the emphasis on the check
Yes, and once she knows the flow by heart she may skip the checklist entirely
No, memory flows are allowed only for emergencies, never for a normal start
quiz.why: Checklists need not be do lists: the actions can be done and the checklist used to confirm them, with emphasis on the check; but checklists have no value if the pilot is not committed to them [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

quiz.q: Per AC 91-55A, which pilot habit best helps catch a starter that keeps running after start?
options: Cycling the master switch off and on after every start to reset the starter relay
Holding the key in START until oil pressure rises, so the starter disengages on its own
Knowing the normal readings, sounds and other indications after a normal start
Leaving starter relay checks to the annual inspection, since pilots cannot detect a stuck relay
quiz.why: A good practice for pilots is to be completely familiar with instrument readings, cockpit sounds and other indicators after normal starts; a change can mean the starter is still running [[18:1|AC 91-55A]].

quiz.q: Which ACS element of this Task names wind as something to consider?
options: K1
S1
R2
S2
quiz.why: S1 is to position the airplane considering structures, other aircraft, wind, and the safety of nearby persons and property (ACS AI.V.C.S1).

quiz.q: During hand propping, where should the descending blade be before the swing?
options: Slightly above horizontal
Slightly below horizontal
Straight down, at the bottom
Straight up
quiz.why: The descending blade is rotated to a position slightly above the horizontal [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

quiz.q: After start, your learner sets 1,000 rpm, but the oil pressure needle has not moved off the bottom of the gauge. What does the AFH say?
options: Add power to about 1,500 rpm so the oil pump can build pressure faster
Taxi out and recheck it at the run-up, where the higher rpm will raise it
Wait for the engine to warm up, since cold oil can take minutes to register
In most conditions it should reach the lower limit within 30 seconds; if it does not, shut down at once
quiz.why: Oil pressure is monitored after start to see that it rises toward the AFM/POH value. In most conditions it should rise to at least the lower limit within 30 seconds, and to prevent damage the engine should be shut down immediately if it does not reach the AFM/POH values within the required time [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's tiedown leaves the trainer right behind a large turboprop that is about to start. What does the AIM say about that position?
options: Prop wash from a turboprop is a hazard only in flight, not on the ramp
Large aircraft blast has overturned or damaged smaller aircraft behind them
A small airplane is safe from blast once its own engine is running
Blast matters only behind jets; turboprop wash is too weak to upset a trainer
final_quiz.why: Prop and jet blast forces generated by large aircraft have overturned or damaged several smaller aircraft taxiing behind them [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]], and blast and prop wash can cause damage and upsets at close range [[33:262|AIM 4-3-18]]. Move the trainer or wait.

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks why she should hold about 1,000 rpm right after start instead of a fast idle to warm up quicker. What is the AFH reason?
options: To charge the battery faster after the heavy draw of the starter
To keep propeller blast and noise low for the people on the ramp
To keep the magnetos and starter cool while the engine warms up
To let oil pressure rise and limit wear from poor lubrication
final_quiz.why: About 1,000 rpm is recommended after start to allow oil pressure to rise and to minimize engine wear from insufficient lubrication at high rpm [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's POH calls for a 2-minute starter cool-down, but the AFH says 30 seconds to 1 minute. What do you teach?
options: The AFH value, because the FAA handbooks override any manufacturer's POH
Either one, since the starter has no real duty limit as long as it is not smoking
The shorter value, to save battery power on a cold morning
The POH value; the AFH notes some AFM/POHs specify longer cool-down routines
final_quiz.why: The AFH gives at least 30 seconds to 1 minute and notes that some AFM/POH specify longer cool-down routines; start procedures come from the AFM/POH [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: Teaching hand propping, why does the AFH want the person out front to leave room to step away as the blade is pulled down?
options: It is a safeguard in case the brakes fail as the engine starts
So the person in the seat can see the blade through the windshield
So the CONTACT call can be heard over the engine noise
To keep from blocking the cooling air flowing into the cowling
final_quiz.why: Allowing space for the person to step away as the propeller is pulled down and the engine starts serves as a safeguard in case the brakes fail [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

final_quiz.q: After a normal-looking start, your learner notices a smell and a light haze of smoke that do not fit a normal start. The gauges look normal. What does the AFH say?
options: Taxi, since the gauges are normal
Shut down and investigate
Add power to clear it
Wait until the run-up to decide
final_quiz.why: Sounds, vibrations, smells or smoke not consistent with normal after-start experience should lead to a shutdown and further investigation [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: In a turboprop start, an unusually high initial fuel flow comes just before the temperature climbs toward its limit. What does the AFH say the pilot should be ready to do?
options: Keep the starter engaged longer to cool the engine
Cut off fuel to the engine
Advance the power lever
Switch from the GPU to the battery
final_quiz.why: The pilot watches for temperatures exceeding limits and is prepared to cut off fuel; unusually high initial fuel flow may be the first sign of a hot start, and serious damage occurs if it continues [[24:306|AFH 15-12]].

final_quiz.q: Why is low battery voltage a special concern for a turboprop start?
options: It drains the boost pump, so the engine gets too little fuel to light off
It leaves the propeller locked on its start locks after the engine lights
It disables the propeller governor, so the blades stay at full pitch
It weakens the compressor rotation and raises the chance of a hot start
final_quiz.why: Low battery voltage greatly diminishes the ability to turn the compressor, and the possibility of damage from a hot start increases [[24:304|AFH 15-10]].

final_quiz.q: At a new airport, the line worker uses some hand signals that differ from the AFH figure. What does the AFH say matters most?
options: Only the AFH signals may be used
Signals are optional when the pilot can see the worker
That a suitable, agreed-upon set of signals is used
Only military signals are standard
final_quiz.why: Whether the AFH set or a modified set is used is not the most important point, as long as a suitable, agreed-upon set of signals is used [[24:52|AFH 2-15]].

final_quiz.q: During a hand propping lesson, the engine does not start. The person out front wants to reposition the blade. What must happen first?
options: Call CONTACT and wait for the reply
Open the throttle slightly for the next try
Verify the magneto switch is OFF
Release the brakes
final_quiz.why: Do not reposition the propeller for another attempt until it is verified that the magneto switch is OFF [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner engages the starter with her feet flat on the floor. What does the AFH say properly working brakes, held before the starter, prevent?
options: The airplane rapidly lunging forward
Overheating of the starter during long cranking
A backfire
A low oil pressure reading in the first 30 seconds
final_quiz.why: Ensuring properly operating brakes are engaged before starter engagement prevents the airplane from rapidly lunging forward [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: Teaching hand propping, why do you correct a learner who stands a full arm's length or more from the blade?
options: He cannot see the pilot or the magneto switch through the windshield
He cannot push the blade fast enough to pull it through the compression stroke
He must lean forward off balance and may fall into the blades as it starts
He cannot hear the CONTACT and SWITCH OFF calls over the wind
final_quiz.why: Too far a stance makes the person lean forward unbalanced, which may cause a fall into the rotating blades; stand slightly less than one arm's length away [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

final_quiz.q: After start, your learner faces a long wait on the ramp in an air-cooled airplane with a constant-speed propeller and cowl flaps. How does the AFH say to set it up for the best cooling?
options: Propeller in full low pitch, nose into the wind, and cowl flaps open
Tail into the wind so the propeller blast carries the heat away from the cowling
Propeller in high pitch and cowl flaps closed so the engine warms evenly
Mixture full rich at 1,700 rpm so more air flows through the cowling
final_quiz.why: Air-cooled engines depend on forward speed for cooling, so during all ground running operate with the propeller in full low pitch, headed into the wind with the cowling installed, and do not close the cowl flaps for warm-up [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your turboprop learner asks what usually causes a hot start. What does the AFH glossary say?
options: A mixture that is too lean in the combustor
An excessively rich mixture in the combustor
Ice in the engine inlet melting during the start
Leaving the ignition on after the engine lights
final_quiz.why: A hot start occurs with normal engine rotation but exhaust temperature above prescribed limits; it is usually caused by an excessively rich mixture in the combustor, and fuel to the engine must be terminated immediately [[24:380|AFH G-8]].

takeaways: The POH start procedures rule; the handbooks add hazard mitigation, and you teach the learner to read and understand both.
Magnetos need no battery: treat every propeller as live, and switch the ignition OFF at shutdown.
Before start: area and behind clear, lights on, CLEAR called and answered, brakes held, hand on the throttle.
After start: about 1,000 rpm, oil pressure within 30 seconds, ammeter shows the starter disengaged, or shut down.
Starter: no more than 30 seconds of cranking, then 30 seconds to 1 minute of cooling; after repeated failures, get help.
Cold, hot, flooded and GPU starts come from the POH; teach them with visualization until the season brings the real thing.
Approach the chocks of a running airplane only from behind the propeller, and agree signals with anyone working at the nose.
cfi_notes: The handbooks give no flooded start procedure and no specific hot start procedure for piston engines. PHAK only warns against overpriming [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]] and lists hot starting as a fuel injection problem [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. Teach the POH procedure for your airplane and say so.

Terminology: the sources use "hot start" only for turbines, as an over-temperature [[24:380|AFH G-8]] [[1:183|PHAK 7-23]]; for pistons the PHAK says "starting a hot engine" [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. Application: say "hot engine start" for pistons to keep the two apart.

The PHAK has the wheels chocked and the brakes set before start [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]; the AFH adds that chocks pulled after start are approached only from behind the propeller, with the throttle at idle [[24:54|AFH 2-17]]. The risk is the person pulling them with the engine running.
Use the AIH runaway engine story [[25:5|AIH 1-1]] in the ground briefing. It makes the mixture-as-backup-stop point better than any lecture.

Sources are thin on GPU risks: only "follow the manufacturer" [[1:190|PHAK 7-30]]. The propeller-arc rule for chocks [[24:54|AFH 2-17]] is the closest stated rule; label your GPU briefing as application of it.

AFH 2-16 says anticollision lights on before every start [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; 14 CFR 91.209(b) requires them lit whenever an equipped aircraft is operated, unless the PIC determines that, because of operating conditions, turning them off is in the interest of safety [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(b)]]. Teach the AFH habit and the CFR exception.

Do not teach hand propping as a workaround for a dead starter in a starter-equipped trainer. The AFH says the starter should work if the airplane is airworthy, and to call a mechanic if not [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Learner on the controls is itself a hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. On first starts keep your feet near the brakes and a hand near the throttle and mixture, and brief who calls a shutdown.
gaps: Exact normal, cold, hot, flooded and GPU start steps, priming strokes, starter limits and warm-up rpm for a given airplane: POH/AFM only.
No source covers the risks of connecting and disconnecting a GPU in detail, or whether to fly after a GPU start on a weak battery; the POH and a mechanic decide.
No source gives a preheat method, time or temperature beyond "approaching and below freezing"; see the POH and the engine maker.
AC 91-13 (cold weather operation) is not among the loaded sources; cold weather starting here rests on the AFH and PHAK only.
The ACS gives no numeric tolerance for S1 or S2.

activities.title: Trace the starting circuit
activities.intro: Drag each part name to its place on the PHAK starting circuit.

activities.title: Which start does it belong to?
activities.intro: Tap each fact, then the start condition the sources tie it to.

items.t: Preheat as temperatures approach and fall below freezing
The primer helps because there is too little heat to vaporize fuel
Fuel can vaporize in the lines before it reaches the cylinders
Listed as a disadvantage of fuel injection
Position lights on as well as anticollision lights
The Emergency Stop signal is used for all stop indications
CONTACT and SWITCH OFF instead of ON and OFF
Firm footing free of gravel, wet grass or ice

activities.title: Teach the first start: lesson order
activities.intro: Put the steps of a first engine start lesson in the order the AIH method gives, then tap Check.
steps: Ground: read the POH start procedure together, cover safety and take questions
You start the engine, narrating each step
The learner calls each step while you start it
The learner starts the engine, thinking out loud
Learner self-assessment, then your assessment, compared

activities.title: Starting numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your learner makes three 30-second cranking attempts with the AFH minimum 30-second cool-down between them. How many seconds from the first crank to the end of the third?
items.why: 3 x 30 s cranking + 2 x 30 s cooling = 90 + 60 = 150 s [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

items.q: Using the longest AFH cool-down (1 minute) between 30-second cranks, how many complete cranking attempts fit in 4 minutes?
items.why: Each attempt after the first adds 60 + 30 = 90 s. 30 + 90(n - 1) must be at most 240, so 90n - 60 at most 240, n at most 3.33, so 3 attempts [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

items.q: The oil pressure needle first rises 12 seconds after start. How many seconds were left before the AFH 30-second shutdown point?

activities.title: True or false: limits and the propeller
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If the master switch is OFF, moving the propeller cannot start the engine.
cards.why: False. Magnetos need no outside power; with the ignition ON the engine can fire [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

cards.s: Under 14 CFR 91.209, position lights must be lit when an aircraft is operated from sunset to sunrise.
cards.why: True [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]. The AFH adds them to the before-start items at night [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

cards.s: Hand propping is safe as long as it is done perfectly.
cards.why: False. Hand propping is a hazardous procedure even when done perfectly [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].

cards.s: Oil temperature may take several minutes or longer to rise after a cold start.
On a turbine engine, temperatures are hotter during starting than at any other time.
When hand propping, the person out front pulls the propeller through to prime the engine before calling BRAKES AND CONTACT.
cards.why: True. After the first callback, the person out front pulls the propeller through to prime the engine, then says BRAKES AND CONTACT [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

activities.title: Match the S1 item to the check
activities.intro: Tap an S1 item, then the check that fits it.

pairs.r: Look at what is behind the airplane before the propeller blast reaches it
Do not start where prop wash or jet blast hits, or is hit by, another airplane at close range
Point the nose into the wind for a ground run
Call CLEAR out the window and wait for a response
Avoid a spot where the propeller will stir up gravel or dust

activities.title: A summer afternoon start, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are giving a dual lesson in a fuel-injected trainer that a renter just flew and parked 20 minutes ago. It is 95 degrees F. Your learner has made only cold-morning starts so far.

steps.s: Before you walk out, what do you do about the start?
options: Nothing; a start is a start
Read the POH hot start procedure with the learner and talk through it
Plan to hand prop if it will not start
Plan to crank until it catches
steps.why: Hot fuel-injected engines can be hard to start and vapor lock on hot days [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]; the procedure comes from the POH [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], and visualization prepares the learner [[25:183|AIH 9-13]].

steps.s: The airplane sits with its tail toward the fuel truck and its driver. What now?
options: Start with low rpm and hope
Start and taxi away fast
Have the truck moved or push the airplane so the blast goes clear
Turn on the strobes as warning
steps.why: Check behind and do not blow debris into persons or property [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]; position the airplane for persons and property (ACS AI.V.C.S1).

steps.s: She cranks 25 seconds with no start and reaches for the primer again. What do you say?
options: Stop, let the starter cool at least 30 seconds to 1 minute, and check the POH hot start steps
Switch magnetos to L and crank
Pump the throttle hard
Prime more and crank again now
steps.why: Starter cool-down of at least 30 seconds to 1 minute [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], and avoid overpriming by following the airplane's priming instructions [[1:185|PHAK 7-25]].

steps.s: The engine catches and surges toward 1,700 rpm. What does she do?
options: Leave it, it will settle
Pull the mixture immediately
Shut off the master
Smoothly reduce to about 1,000 rpm or the POH value
steps.why: About 1,000 rpm after start to let oil pressure rise [[24:53|AFH 2-16]], with slow, smooth throttle movement [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].

steps.s: The engine runs smoothly. The line worker walks toward the nosewheel to pull the chock. What do you have your learner do?
options: Wave him in from the front so she can see him
Throttle to idle, and the worker approaches the chock only from behind the propeller
Add power so the propeller is easier to see
Nothing; chocks are the worker's job
steps.why: The propeller is nearly invisible; before the chocks are removed the throttle is set to idle and the chocks are approached only from the rear of the propeller, never from the front or side [[24:54|AFH 2-17]].
